title: Five times as many fast marathons
p1: Each bar counts the men's marathons run in under 2:07 that year.
p2: For fifteen years only a select few broke 2:07 - around twenty runs a season. Then the first carbon-plated 'super shoes' went on sale in 2017 and the bars took off, even in 2020, when the pandemic wiped out most of the big-city races. When World Athletics stepped in to regulate the shoes, it set the limits high enough to keep them legal.

title: Six times as many fast marathons
p1: Each bar counts the women's marathons run in under 2:24 that year.
p2: Before 2017, sub-2:24 was rare air: fewer than twenty runs in a typical year. The super-shoe era changed that even faster than in the men's race. Since 2022 there have been more than a hundred a year. When World Athletics stepped in to regulate the shoes, it set the limits high enough to keep them legal.

title: Faster all the way down the list
p1: Records get the attention, but look further down. The lines show how much quicker the 10th and 100th fastest men's marathons of each year were than in 2001.
p2: A first wave came with big-city races and pacemakers around 2007-12, then progress stalled. After 2017 it picked up again and went deep into the field: 2025's 100th-fastest time would have ranked 24th in 2015.

title: Women's times fell even further
p1: The lines show how much quicker the 10th and 100th fastest women's marathons of each year were than in 2001.
p2: The women's 10th-fastest time actually got slower between 2012 and 2016. Then the shoes arrived. Since 2016 the 100th-fastest time has dropped by more than four and a half minutes, and 2025's 100th-fastest would have ranked 13th in 2015.

title: Where: the Valencia effect
p1: Bubbles show where the men's elite marathons were run each year. Bigger bubble, more of them.
p2: Valencia hardly featured before 2019. Since 2020 it has staged more sub-2:07 runs than anywhere else: a flat course, cool December weather, and pacemakers and prize money built around records. So part of the speed-up is simply runners choosing faster courses.

title: Where: Valencia takes over from London
p1: Bubbles show where the women's elite marathons were run each year. Bigger bubble, more of them.
p2: London was the women's fast course of the 2000s and 2010s. Since 2020 Valencia has taken over, with Berlin and London close behind and Tokyo now a regular stop for fast women's times. So part of the speed-up is simply runners choosing faster courses.

title: Who: Kenya's grip loosens
p1: Each bar splits an era's elite men's marathons by the runner's nation.
p2: Before 2017 nearly two in every three were run by Kenyans. Ethiopia has since drawn level, and more fast times now come from everywhere else - Japan's deep domestic marathon scene, Europe, the USA.

title: Who: Ethiopia leads the way
p1: Each bar splits an era's elite women's marathons by the runner's nation.
p2: Ethiopian women have run the biggest share in every era, with Kenya second. Japan's share was larger in the 2000s, the era of Olympic champion Mizuki Noguchi, and the rest of the world is catching up again.

title: A door that opened
p1: The area shows how many men broke 2:07 for the first time each year.
p2: Before the shoes, around nine new names a year joined the club. Over the last five years it's been closer to forty - athletes who ten years earlier might never have run a time anyone noticed.

title: A door that opened
p1: The area shows how many women broke 2:24 for the first time each year.
p2: Before 2017 the club gained about seven new members a year. Since 2022 it's been more than thirty a year. That's a lot of new names.

title: The same jump in the half marathon
p1: If the shoes are the main driver, the effect should show up over other distances too. Each line compares a year's elite runs with that event's 2001-16 average (half marathon: under 60:00).
p2: Men's elite half marathons were already growing in the late 2000s, but both events take off again after 2017. Since 2020 there have been about three and a half times as many elite half marathons as the old average, and five times as many marathons. Courses and nations explain part of the change. The timing - the same years, across distances - points firmly at the shoes.

title: The same jump, only bigger
p1: If the shoes are the main driver, the effect should show up over other distances too. Each line compares a year's elite runs with that event's 2001-16 average (half marathon: under 67:00).
p2: Sub-67 half marathons were almost unheard of before 2017 - around two a year. Now there are more than thirty a year, an even steeper climb than in the marathon. Courses and nations explain part of the change. The timing - the same years, across distances - points firmly at the shoes.

title: AT THE FINISH
p1: The shoes made the best runners quicker, but the bigger change is how many good runners they turned into world-class ones. Faster courses and a wider pool of countries helped too. A 2:06 men's marathon would have ranked 11th in the world in 2015. In 2025 it ranked 64th.
